what_it_does: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models — language models where only a small subset of specialized sub-networks ('experts') activates for each input token — are too large to fit on typical GPUs in their original precision. Storing each weight as a 3-bit integer (instead of the usual 16-bit float) would slash memory use, but existing 3-bit compression destroys accuracy and lacks GPU kernels that actually run faster at batch size greater than one. MiLo solves both problems: it uses small correction matrices to repair the accuracy damage, and it introduces the first 3-bit GPU kernel that achieves real measured speedups for batched inference.
method_in_detail:
The observation. When you store a weight as a very small integer, the rounding error is not uniform: extreme outlier values get captured reasonably well, but the many moderate values in the middle of the distribution lose detail. This error can be represented as a residual matrix — the difference between the original weight and the rounded version. That residual matrix is often low-rank, meaning it can be approximated compactly as the product of two small matrices.

How MiLo works. Step 1 — quantize: Apply a calibration-free quantization algorithm (HQQ, which fits a statistical distribution to the weights rather than needing sample data) to compress each weight matrix to 3-bit integers. Step 2 — compensate: Compute the residual (original minus compressed), then use SVD (singular value decomposition — a standard math technique that finds the best low-rank approximation) to build a small correction matrix U×V. At inference time, the output is computed as: (3-bit-weight decoded to float) + U×V. Step 3 — iterate: Jointly re-optimize the quantized weights and the correction matrices together in alternating rounds until the combined error stops shrinking, typically converging in about 20 iterations.

Key design choice — adaptive rank. MoE models have two fundamentally different kinds of layers: dense layers (like attention projections) that process every token, and sparse expert layers that only activate occasionally. Dense layers are far more rank-sensitive (a small correction matrix helps them much more), so MiLo gives them higher ranks. Among experts, those activated more frequently get more rank budget. Within any layer, weights with heavier-tailed distributions (measured by statistical kurtosis — how 'spiky' the distribution is) get more rank because they suffer more from rounding.

The GPU kernel. 32 consecutive 3-bit values are packed losslessly into three 32-bit integers (zero wasted bits). Dequantization uses bit-manipulation tricks rather than slow type conversions, processing two values simultaneously per register. Weights are loaded asynchronously from GPU memory while the previous batch of values is being computed, hiding memory latency. MoE-specific tile shapes reduce synchronization overhead for the smaller matrices found in expert layers.

The result. On Mixtral-8×7B (a 47-billion-parameter MoE model), MiLo recovers over 87% of the accuracy lost by 3-bit compression, with only 1.4% additional memory versus a plain 3-bit baseline. The custom kernel delivers 1.2–1.26x speedup over the previous best 4-bit kernel (MARLIN) even at batch sizes greater than one.
